items.title: Territorial Acknowledgement
notes: Mayor McCabe opened the meeting with the following Territorial Acknowledgement:

We would like to begin by acknowledging that the land on which we gather (land on which we are broadcasting from) today is the land traditionally cared for by the Haudenosaunee, Anishinaabe and Chonnontan People. We also acknowledge the enduring presence and deep traditional knowledge and philosophies of the Indigenous People with whom we share this land today.
Tomorrow, March 31st, is National Indigenous Languages Day.

There are over 60 unique Indigenous language dialects spoken in Canada, and all are considered to be critically endangered, except the dialects of Inuktitut. The number of Indigenous language speakers continues to decline. Contact between Indigenous and European languages has led to the borrowing of many Indigenous words into English and French as well as the creation of new language varieties.
There has been a continued dedication to the reclamation and revitalization of Indigenous languages.

With respect to my personal and professional reconciliation journey, I grew up on a farm outside of Kenilworth, Ontario. The land was also the traditional territory of the Anishinaabe and Haudenosaunee people. My grandparents owned this farm and my parents purchased it when they got married.
The area was covered by multiple treaties, most notably Treaty 45.5 signed in 1836, also known as the Saugeen Tract Purchase.

Historically, this area was utilized by the Attawandaron people however, according to research, the confederacy was dispersed in the mid 17th century by disease and war with the Haudenosaunee – around 1653. The land was heavily surveyed and described as “empty wilderness waiting for European settlement.” By 1836, the culture of the Attawandaron and the Haudenosaunee people was considered destroyed.
As Mayor, I continue my learning and reconciliation journey.

I’ve walked in UW’s Truth and Reconciliation Walks, helped paint a bit of Laurier’s beautiful First Nations mural, attended local Pow Wows and City of Waterloo Museum exhibits, and participated in training opportunities about Sacred Fires. I’ve read local authors, such as North Wind Man, and other authors, notably Tanya Talaga. Seven Fallen Feathers particularly has stayed with me. I’ve toured the Mohawk Institute Residential School aka the MUSH Hole, in Brantford, that operated until June 27, 1970 as Canada’s longest running residential school, running for 142 years.

Now it is the Woodland Cultural Centre, and again, I encourage everyone to make time to go to this important centre. I’m grateful for the advice and work of Indigenous Advisor Brian Hill, his work at the City, and with the Association of Municipalities of Ontario on AMO’s first Indigenous Action Plan.
Over my 3 years, I’ve met with Six Nations of the Grand River Chief Hill, Mississauga’s of the Credit former Chief Sault as well as local First Nations’ leaders:

Donna Dubie, Healing of the Seven Generations; Elder Mygeeun Henry, UW Indigenous Advisor; Dr. Darin Johnston, Laurier VP Indigenous Affairs; Professor Clarence Cachagee, Crowshield Lodge; Bangishimo and Amy Smoke, Land Back;

White Owl Mike Duke; Anastasia Lyons, Firekeeper; Laury Turcotte, KW Urban Native Wigwam; Tina Rowe, Southwestern Ontario Aboriginal Health Access Centre; Renata Richards, Healing of the Seven Generations and others.

I’m grateful that they offered the opportunity to continue to build our relationship and to meet each season. Very soon, I will again meet with Chief Hill as she continues to meet with Mayors in each of the 47 municipalities in the Haldimand Tract.
I’m grateful for the time, the patience and the learning that every First Nations’ leader and resident has provided me.
Of course, there is more to do. And I remain committed to learning.

5. MOMENT OF REFLECTION Continued
Mayor McCabe added an additional moment of reflection for Transgender Day of Visibility:

Today is the International Transgender Day of Visibility. This annual awareness day honors the lives of transgender people while shedding light on the discrimination and challenges they continue to face. Visibility plays a crucial role in challenging the stigma and misconceptions surrounding transgender people. It also emphasizes the diversity within the transgender community, reminding us that transgender individuals are not a monolithic group but rather a vibrant community with many different experiences, identities and needs. As a community, we’re committed to fostering safe spaces for self- discovery and taking action on oppressive systems that perpetrate violence and harm.

items.title: Zoning By-law Amendment Z-25-22,
notes: BlackDoor (Westhill) Inc., 36 Westhill Drive
Report No.: IPPW2026-014
Prepared By: Aminu Bello
Ward No.: Ward 1 – Southwest

Aminu Bello gave a presentation outlining the proposed development, with details on the subject lands, planning framework, and the revisions to the design that were made since the Informal Meeting. He then responded to questions of Council. Ron Ormson also responded to questions of Council.

Kristen Barisdale, GSP Group, gave a presentation further detailing the development, with additional information on the revisions and the updates to include more family-friendly amenities, along with a rooftop terrace. Kristen Barisdale then responded to questions of Council.
Sabahvr Rahma, Resident of Waterloo spoke against the proposed development, expressing that residents’ concerns around height and density have not been adequately addressed in the revised proposal.
Aminu Bello responded to questions of Council.

items.title: Questions
notes: Councillor Freeman asked a question of staff regarding the density of signs and posters that are put up in the right-of-way, and if Municipal Enforcement has the right tools to deal with them. Kevin Van Ooteghem responded that he’d take it away and follow up at a later date.

items.title: New Business
notes: As a member of the Board and Large Urban Caucus Chair, Mayor McCabe gave Council an update on the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), including changes to AMO’s communications and how they manage their procurement processes.

Councillor Freeman mentioned that she and Chris Hodgson would be speaking at the Ontario Good Roads Association Conference on March 31 regarding the City’s Bicycle Friendly Communities designation and encouraging other municipalities to consider becoming bike friendly communities.
Councillor Wright wanted to draw attention to the Uptown Egg Hunt, hosted by the Uptown BIA, taking place on April 11.
